To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the use of composted duck manure enriched wood shaving compost and the organic fraction from source-separated municipal solid wastes in the growing media of tomato plants, resulted in higher fruit yields than those obtained with commercially available growing media, and the same or higher yields than those obtained using black earth/sandy loam soil.
substrates based on duck manure enriched wood shavings compost (DMC), and the organic fraction from source-separated municipal solid wastes compost (MSW) are suitable for growing tomatoes.
the composted duck manure and source-separated municipal waste compost were suitable for tomato production in the greenhouse.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the use of organic substrates for the cultivation of tomato in a protected environment and shows the potential of using DMC and MSWC in a mixture with brick dust and/or plastic as a substitute of peat.
the development of a new substrate for tomato production that is environmentally friendly and economically viable.
a sustainable use of organic waste, such as source-separated MSW composts and poultry excreta enriched substrates, as growth media for horticultural crops.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
composting is a viable option for recycling source-separated MSW, as well as duck excreta, and that these composts can be safely used for the production of tomato plants.
the use of substrates made with composts from DMC and MSWs is an environmentally sound alternative to the traditional use of peat-based mixes for the production of tomato plants.
substrates A and B were the most suitable for the growth of tomato in the greenhouse.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

composted substrates A, containing 3:2 proportion of DMC/MSW composts and substrates B and C, with the addition of 15% (by weight) of brick dust or shredded plastics, respectively, are suitable substrates for the cultivation of tomato plants in a greenhouse.
the use of duck excreta and source-separated municipal waste composts in growing mixes for horticultural crops is an effective and sustainable practice.
substrates A (3:2 DMC and MSWC) and B (A + 15% brick dust) were the best substrates for the growth and yield performance of tomato.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the combination of DMC and source-separated municipal waste composts can be used as an effective and sustainable alternative for peat-based growing substrates.
the use of substrates made from duck excreta and MSW compost, in combination with a mineral fertilizer, is an alternative for the production of tomato in greenhouse conditions.
composted substrates can be used for tomato cultivation, with the added benefit of reducing the amount of waste that is disposed of in landfills.
